title: The agent loop: think, act, observe (ReAct)
notes: ReAct, short for reason and act, is the agent loop: think, act, observe, and repeat until the job is done.
Your code runs the loop and the tools; the model decides each step, and a trace shows why.
Every loop needs a step limit in code, and an honest hand-off with a summary when it is reached.

slides.title: The agent loop: think, act, observe (ReAct)
slides.sub: The loop at the heart of every agent, and the limit that keeps it safe
sentences: This is the last lesson of the module, and it ties everything together.
Memory, retrieval and planning all run inside one loop.
You will learn how the loop works, how to read it, and why it always needs a limit.

slides.title: Reason and act
slides.definition: Reason and act: the agent thinks about the next step, takes one action, observes the result, and repeats.

analogy.label: Think of it as
analogy.text: A cook tasting as they go: season, taste, adjust, taste again, and stop when it's right.

sentences: The pattern is called react, short for reason and act.
First the agent thinks: given what it knows, what's the next step?
Then it acts, usually by calling one tool.
Then it observes: it reads the tool's result and adds it to what it knows.
Think of a cook tasting as they go. Season, taste, adjust, and stop when it's right.

slides.title: The loop

note.text: Your code runs the loop. The model decides each step.

sentences: Drawn as a loop, it looks like this.
Think: Scout looks at the conversation and the results so far, and decides what to do next.
Act: it asks for a tool, and your code runs it.
Observe: the result goes back into the messages, so Scout can read it.
Then a check: is the job done? If yes, Scout replies. If not, it goes round again.
Notice who does what. Your code runs the loop, and the model decides each step.

slides.title: Reading a ReAct trace

messages.label: Ana
messages.text: Swap my tent for the 3-person one and tell me when it arrives. ORB-10482.

messages.label: Think
messages.text: Plan: check her order, then the 3-person tent's stock.

messages.label: Think
messages.text: No swap possible today. Offer: keep the 2P, or return it within 30 days.

messages.label: Reply
messages.text: Sorry, Ana, the 3-person tent is sold out. Your 2-person tent is on its way: you can keep it, or return it within 30 days of delivery.

sentences: Here's Ana's request again, this time as a trace of the loop.
Scout thinks first: check the order, then the stock.
It acts with the get order tool, and observes that her two-person tent has shipped.
It acts again with check stock, and observes a zero.
It thinks again with the new fact: the swap can't happen today, so it changes course.
Finally it replies with options, and the loop ends.
Reading a trace like this, step by step, is how you will debug agents in Module 5.

slides.title: The loop in your code
slides.lead: You wrote this loop in Module 3. Each part maps to think, act or observe.

rows.out: the loop, with a hard limit
think: the model picks its next move
act: your code runs the tool
observe: results go back to the model

aside.label: Done
aside.text: When stop_reason isn't tool_use, the model has answered and the loop breaks.

sentences: Good news: you already wrote this loop in Module 3.
The for loop allows a fixed number of steps, and no more.
Each call to messages create is a think: the model reads everything and picks its next move.
When it asks for a tool, your run tool function is the act.
Appending the results to the messages is the observe step.
And when the stop reason is anything other than tool use, the model has answered, and the loop ends.

slides.title: Why the loop needs a limit

note.text: Six steps covers almost every Orbit request. If Scout needs more, a person should look.

sentences: Every loop needs a way out that doesn't depend on the model.
If the tracking service keeps timing out, a loop with no limit can retry all night.
If an item is out of stock, an agent can re-plan in circles, trying the same idea again and again.
And if the model misreads a result, it may repeat the same call over and over.
A step limit puts a hard ceiling on the time and the cost of every message.
Six steps covers almost every Orbit request. If Scout needs more, a person should take a look.

slides.title: When the limit is hit

note.text: Tell the customer the truth: a teammate is on it. Never a guess dressed up as an answer.

sentences: So what should happen when the limit is reached?
The loop has used its last step, and the job still isn't done.
Your code stops it. No more tool calls, whatever the model asks for.
It writes a short summary: what the customer asked, what was tried, and what failed.
Then it hands the case to a person, who starts from that summary instead of from scratch.
And the customer hears the truth: a teammate is picking this up. Never a guess dressed up as an answer.

slides.title: What to take away

points.text: ReAct: think, act, observe, and repeat until the job is done.
Your code runs the loop; the model decides each step.
A trace shows exactly why the agent did what it did.
Always a step limit, with an honest hand-off when it's hit.

sentences: Let's recap the module's last idea.
React, short for reason and act, means think, act, observe, and repeat until the job is done.
Your code runs the loop, and the model decides each step inside it.
A trace of those steps shows you exactly why the agent did what it did.
Every loop gets a step limit, with an honest hand-off when it's reached.
Now watch Scout do all of this, then build it yourself.

midQuiz.q: In the ReAct loop, what happens in the observe step?
options: The model reads the tool's result and updates what it knows
Your code shows the customer each tool call
The model checks its reply for typos
midQuiz.explain: Observe means the tool result goes back into the messages, so the model's next think starts from the new facts.
midQuiz.hint: Observe comes right after act. What does an act produce?

midQuiz.q: In your Python loop, which line is the act step?
midQuiz.explain: The model only asks for a tool. Your code acts: run_tool is the line that actually runs it.
midQuiz.hint: Which line actually does something in the world?

endQuiz.q: Why should the step limit live in your code, not only in the prompt?
options: The prompt has no room for numbers
Code enforces it even when the model keeps asking for tools
The model can't count past five
endQuiz.explain: A prompt is a request that a stuck model may not follow. A for loop with a limit always stops.
endQuiz.hint: Which one still works when the model is confused?

endQuiz.q: Scout reaches step 6 of 6 without finishing. What should happen?
options: Raise the limit and keep going
Stop, summarise what was tried, and hand off to a person
Reply with the most likely answer
endQuiz.explain: The limit did its job. A summary and an honest hand-off beat both an endless loop and a guess.
endQuiz.hint: What would Leo's team need to pick the case up?
